question: What is the primary advantage of giving medications through the oral route?

options.B: It is the most convenient and common way
options.D: It works faster than intravenous injections

explanation: The oral route is favored because patients can usually swallow pills themselves, making it easy and convenient for long-term care. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why should a nurse avoid crushing an enteric-coated tablet?

options.A: It turns the solid pill into an unmixable powder
options.B: It changes the color of the liquid mixture
options.C: It causes the medication to dissolve too slowly
options.D: It ruins the special coating designed to protect the stomach

explanation: Enteric coatings protect the stomach lining from irritation or protect the drug from stomach acid; crushing destroys this barrier. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why must a nurse position a patient upright before giving oral medications?

options.A: It speeds up the first-pass metabolism in the liver
options.B: It allows the nurse to check the pulse more easily
options.C: Gravity helps the medication go down safely and prevents choking
options.D: It stops the stomach acid from rising into the throat

explanation: Sitting at a 90-degree angle uses gravity to guide the pill into the esophagus and protects the airway from accidental aspiration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: What vital sign must a nurse always check before administering certain heart medications like digoxin?
explanation: Certain cardiac drugs lower the heart rate, so nurses must measure the pulse beforehand to ensure it is safe to give. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: How many patient identifiers should a nurse check before giving a medication?
explanation: Using identifiers like the patient's name and hospital number ensures the right person receives the treatment. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: When is the best time for a nurse to document that a medication was given?

options.A: While walking down the hallway to the room
options.B: Right before taking the pills out of the drawer
options.C: At the very end of the entire work shift
options.D: Immediately after the patient swallows the drug

explanation: Documenting right away prevents accidental double-dosing and ensures an accurate record of care. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: Why should a nurse avoid using household kitchen spoons to measure liquid medications?

options.A: Using them makes the liquid spill on the table
options.B: Household spoons react chemically with liquid drugs
options.C: Kitchen spoons are too heavy for patients to hold
options.D: Kitchen spoons vary in size and give inaccurate doses

explanation: Household spoons are not standardized for medical measurements, which can lead to giving too much or too little medicine. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: Where should a nurse look when measuring liquid medication in a clear plastic cup?

options.A: At eye level with the bottom of the liquid meniscus
options.B: From underneath the table looking up through the plastic
options.C: From high above looking down at the top of the fluid
options.D: At the highest edge of the liquid touching the cup wall

explanation: Reading at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus ensures the exact volume of medication is measured. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why must a nurse stay at the bedside until the patient swallows all their medications?

options.A: To record the exact second the patient stops drinking water
options.B: To collect payment for the hospital prescription fees
options.C: To make sure the water cup is returned clean to the medication room
options.D: To confirm the patient actually takes the drugs and does not hide them

explanation: Staying at the bedside ensures compliance and safety, preventing patients from pocketing pills or missing doses. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take before preparing medications?
explanation: Hand hygiene is the primary step in infection control to prevent spreading germs to clean medication supplies. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: A confused elderly patient keeps holding pills in their cheek without swallowing them. What is this behavior called?
explanation: Pouching happens when patients store food or medication in their cheek pockets instead of swallowing it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which food choice is generally NOT recommended when mixing crushed medication for an infant?

options.A: A small taste of flavored pudding
options.C: Daily milk or formula bottle feeds
options.D: A small drop of fruit puree

explanation: Mixing drugs into routine milk feeds can cause the infant to reject their primary nutrition if the taste changes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is the main reason a nurse performs a follow-up check after giving medication?

options.A: To ask the patient to sign the hospital billing forms
options.B: To evaluate if the drug is working and watch for side effects
options.C: To remind the doctor when the next shift starts
options.D: To clean up the leftover water cups from the bedside table

explanation: Follow-up monitoring ensures therapeutic effectiveness and catches early signs of adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)

question: What action should a nurse take immediately if a medication administration error occurs?

options.A: Ask the patient to keep quiet about the mistake
options.B: Hide the empty medicine cup in the trash can
options.C: Wait until the end of the month to see if harm happens
options.D: Report it to the doctor and nurse manager right away

explanation: Immediate reporting ensures the patient gets quick medical evaluation and treatment if an adverse effect develops. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)
